changes.before: Create Counter(5), then call AddPoint twice. Which value can outside code read from Score?
changes.after: Let other code read a score while the class controls changes.

before: A property offers accessors for reading or writing a value. In public int Score { get; private set; }, get permits outside reads; private set permits writes only inside this class.
The constructor and AddPoint method can change Score because they belong to Counter. Outside code may call AddPoint but may not assign counter.Score directly.
This is an auto-implemented property: the compiler supplies its storage. A method can preserve a rule while changing it; this example allows only one-point increments after construction.
Expected behavior from this example: 3. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Add a public Reset method that sets Score to zero without making its setter public. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A property provides a way to read or write an object's value. get allows reading. This public Score property can be read by code outside Counter.
private set allows writing only inside the class. Outside code cannot directly assign a new value to counter.Score.
The constructor can set the starting score. AddPoint can increase it because both belong to Counter. Outside code can ask for that change by calling AddPoint.
The program prints 3. The constructor starts Score at 2, and AddPoint increases it once.
This short property lets the compiler supply its storage. Keeping its setter private makes callers use the class's update methods. Here, the only update method adds one point.
